title: The Skill That Got Me Promoted Was the One I Had to Give Up
author: Kelly Mackin
summary: Kelly Mackin recounts the leadership inflection point she faced in her late twenties when a trusted mentor told her that the perfectionist execution she had built her career on was the very thing that would cap it. She had constructed her reputation on flawlessness—checking every number, never missing—and was advised that scaling required letting others carry details she had always held herself. When she tested that advice by letting her team build a presentation without her review, an executive spotted an error in front of the most powerful leader in the building. The essay traces her decision not to retreat to control despite the humiliation, and describes two practical responses: publicly owning the miss in front of her team while reframing the standard ('we never want a small error to cloud a strong message'), and building a collaborative red-pen review process that distributed quality ownership across the group. Her central insight is that when you check everything yourself, all errors feel equally fatal and you lose your sense of proportion—only by stepping back do you learn to distinguish real problems from small ones. Leadership at scale requires transferring your highest-held individual strength into a team system.
points: The skill that produces early-career success—individual flawlessness—actively prevents leadership scaling, because you cannot be the person with hands on every detail and the person trusted with something bigger than yourself.

The specific heat of being caught in an error after finally letting go feels like proof you should never have loosened your grip, but it is actually the moment that teaches you to distinguish real problems from small ones.

Rather than retreating to control after the presentation error, Mackin publicly owned the miss, attributed it to a still-manual process rather than team failure, and protected the team's ownership of the excellent work they had built.

Building a 'red pen lunch'—where the whole team reviewed every number together before high-stakes presentations—transferred quality ownership from one person's eyes to the group, making the bar collectively held.
When you catch everything yourself, every error feels equally fatal and you have no sense of proportion; stepping back is how you develop the ability to see which details actually matter.
quotes: Someone once told me, plainly, that the thing I was best at was the thing that would keep me from being promoted.

Sit with how that lands when you are twenty-eight and everything you are proud of is your own flawlessness. I was not being told to improve. I was being told to give up the one thing that had gotten me everything so far. It felt less like advice and more like being told the ground I was standing on was the problem.

That thought is the whole reason this is hard. In the moment you finally loosen your grip and something goes wrong, it does not feel like a lesson about growth. It feels like proof that you should never have loosened it in the first place.

If I could not let go, I could not scale. And if I could not scale, I could not lead. I would spend my whole career as the most reliable individual performer in the building, valuable and capped, doing more and more of the same work, never trusted with more, because everything I touched required me to touch it. Perfection is an individual sport.

When you check everything yourself, every error feels equally fatal. A typo and a broken model feel the same in your stomach, because your name is on all of it and you cannot tell the difference between what matters and what does not. You have no sense of proportion, because proportion is a thing you can only develop from a little distance.
It felt like losing myself. It was the beginning of actually being able to lead.
